Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The defense sector's AI infrastructure is largely transparent through federal procurement systems. SAM.gov serves as the primary record of solicitations and contract awards, centralizing all federal contract opportunities and registrations where vendors compete for defense work. USAspending makes every federal award downloadable, tracing spending on AI-related solutions back to the underlying Federal Procurement Data System, which records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level. These three platforms—SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS—form the foundational data layer for understanding where defense dollars flow and which companies win contracts.

The Defense Innovation Unit functions as the commercial gateway for AI entry into DoD programs, with public project listings that show how entrepreneurial products are converted into combat capability. Govini operates a decision-science platform built on the federal procurement record, tracking procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy, and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. These tools allow both internal and external stakeholders to monitor real-time patterns in defense AI deployment without requiring classified access.

Government AI laboratories occupy a distinct institutional position separate from commercial vendors. The two catalogued government labs—Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China—represent different political economies. Both can command sovereign budget commitments and infrastructure for compute and facilities that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. State-funded government labs carry public mandates and draw on government budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build and the priorities they serve.

The specific applications of AI in defense concentrate on decision support, autonomy, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance processing as programs of record. Govini's platform layer transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. This pattern reflects the sector's emphasis on real-time readiness, supply-chain visibility, and resource optimization across military operations.

Silicon Valley Defense Group and Janes represent the analyst layer covering commercial entrants and the broader defense-industrial base. Janes applies tradecraft to validated intelligence on military platforms and threat intelligence, maintaining one of the largest global datasets of defense capabilities and vendor activity. Long-running subscription analysts like Janes and Forecast International provide forecasts and procurement intelligence that complement the free public data systems, offering context on contractor performance and program trajectories that shape investment decisions.

Regulatory posture in defense AI remains embedded in federal acquisition rules and Controlled Unclassified Information protocols. SAM.gov and related systems are restricted to authorized users and subject to monitoring, with all individuals viewing procurement data required to protect Controlled Unclassified Information in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002. The transition of FPDS.gov's retirement into SAM.gov reflects ongoing modernization of federal systems, consolidating contract management under a single platform while maintaining security and compliance requirements specific to national defense work.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: According to The World of AI, two government labs are listed: the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. Both are state-funded, carry public mandates, and rely on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital, which shapes their research priorities. The Abu Dhabi lab operates under the Advanced Technology Research Council and has released frontier open models, while the Shanghai lab is backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, aligning it with China’s central research agenda. Each lab can command infrastructure commitments, such as compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. The page also notes that these entries are individually verified, rebuilt daily from primary sources, and lists books by Stephen R. Jordan.
